articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities in Latest Counter Terrorism Action
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations today as part of its ongoing counter-terrorism efforts. Details of the specific individuals and entities targeted were released, underscoring the U.S. government's commitment to disrupting terrorist financing and support networks globally.

These designations aim to isolate those involved in terrorist activities from the international financial system. The action highlights the continuous vigilance required to combat evolving threats and protect national security interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Guatemalan Drug Trafficking Organizations with Terrorist Ties
body: The U.S. Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has added Guatemala's Los Lorenzanas organization and Los Mendoza Drug Trafficking Organization to its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. These designations expose both groups to secondary sanctions risk under Executive Order 13224, as amended by EO 13886.

Los Lorenzanas was identified as a transnational terrorist group, while Los Mendoza was linked to Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel. OFAC also amended the listing of Guatemala's Los Huistas organization to include the same secondary sanctions exposure, citing its ties to both the Sinaloa Cartel and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

These actions aim to extend the reach of U.S. sanctions to non-U.S. parties dealing with these groups, thereby increasing pressure on Central American trafficking networks. This move is expected to prompt banks and other counterparties to reassess their exposure to the named organizations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran Designation Update
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has released an update regarding Iran designations. This action is part of the ongoing efforts to address the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities and its support for terrorism.

The update clarifies existing designations and may include new entries or modifications to previously listed individuals and entities. Such updates are crucial for maintaining the effectiveness of sanctions programs and ensuring compliance by financial institutions and businesses.

articles.headline: New Iran-Related Designations Announced by OFAC
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. These actions are part of the U.S. government's comprehensive strategy to counter the Iranian regime's illicit activities, including its nuclear program, support for regional proxies, and human rights abuses.

The designations aim to further restrict the Iranian government's access to the international financial system and its ability to fund its malign activities. Entities and individuals found to be supporting these activities are subject to asset blocking and other prohibitions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations. This action aims to disrupt illicit financial networks and cyber threats that pose risks to U.S. national security and economic stability.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also imposed new sanctions related to Cuba and published a Cuba-related determination. These measures reinforce existing policies aimed at promoting democracy and human rights in Cuba, while also addressing the Cuban government's support for malign actors.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating cybercrime and transnational criminal enterprises, as well as its continued pressure on the Cuban regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran Sanctions, Amends Venezuela General License, and Issues Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and updated certain Iran-related listings. These actions are part of the U.S. government's ongoing efforts to counter the Iranian regime's destabilizing activities.

In addition, OFAC published an Iran-related alert to provide guidance on potential sanctions risks. Concurrently, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) were issued, providing clarity on authorized transactions and compliance expectations for activities involving Venezuela.

These measures reflect the U.S. government's dynamic approach to sanctions, adapting to evolving geopolitical landscapes and ensuring that sanctions remain effective tools for foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1 for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran General License FF-1, titled "Authorizing the Wind Down of Transactions Involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance."

This amended general license provides a specific timeframe and authorization for the wind-down of certain transactions, allowing for an orderly cessation of activities involving the designated entity. This action aims to minimize undue impact on legitimate humanitarian and commercial activities while ensuring the effectiveness of sanctions.

The issuance of such general licenses is a common practice by OFAC to provide clarity and manage the implementation of sanctions programs, allowing affected parties to adjust their operations accordingly.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates North Korea IT Worker Facilitators and DRC-Related Entities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in facilitating North Korean IT worker fraud, which aims to generate revenue for the DPRK's illicit weapons programs. Among those added to the SDN list are First Financial and Technical Development Center, based in North Korea and Vladivostok, Russia, along with several Russian and North Korean individuals.

These individuals, including Ilya Aleksandrovich Boykov, Han Yu Song, and Ri Thae Chol, are identified as operating in Russia and facilitating DPRK IT worker activities. The designations carry secondary sanctions risk under North Korea Sanctions Regulations.

In a separate action, OFAC also imposed designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), targeting entities and individuals supporting destabilizing activities in the region. These actions underscore the U.S. commitment to countering threats to international security and stability.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-headquartered cloud networking solutions provider. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and related services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to being majority-owned by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not independently listed on the SDN List until 2022.

OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. This case highlights the importance of thorough due diligence, especially in acquisitions, to identify blocked entities even when they are not directly listed on sanctions lists.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) as part of its ongoing review to ensure published guidance remains current. The updated FAQs cover topics related to blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC.

Specifically, OFAC amended 11 FAQs, including those addressing jurisdictions subject to broad sanctions, procedures for blocking accounts and funds transfers, interest requirements on blocked funds, and when to reject rather than block a transaction. The revisions also clarify notification procedures for customers when property is blocked and the timing and format for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions.

These amendments aim to provide greater clarity for financial institutions and other entities on their compliance obligations, particularly regarding the nuances of handling sanctions-related transactions and reporting requirements.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined Over $1.5 Million by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The violations involved the export of networking equipment and related services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), between September 2018 and March 2022.

MMZA was deemed a blocked entity by operation of law due to being majority-owned by the designated JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not directly listed on the SDN List until 2022. OFAC determined that these apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious.

This enforcement action underscores the critical importance of robust sanctions compliance programs, particularly in the context of mergers and acquisitions, to identify and mitigate risks associated with indirectly owned entities.

articles.headline: UK Inflation Rises to 3.6% in October, Driven by Record Fuel Prices Amid Iran War
body: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.6% in October, up from 3.5% in September, primarily driven by a significant increase in petrol and diesel prices. Figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS) indicate that diesel prices hit a record high, and petrol prices reached their highest level in four years, largely due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East involving Iran.

The rise in fuel costs was the major contributor to the headline inflation rate, which is now at its highest level in a year. This increase puts further pressure on the Bank of England to consider raising interest rates as households brace for higher energy bills this winter, with forecasts suggesting a 26% rise in energy bills from January.

Services inflation remained steady at 3.7%, while food prices saw their slowest rate of increase since September 2021. The annual costs of raw materials and goods leaving factories also continued to climb, influenced by rising energy and crude oil prices.

articles.headline: Euro Area Annual Inflation Climbs to 4.0% in October
body: The annual inflation rate in the euro area reached 4.0% in October 2026, an increase from 3.8% in September, according to Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union. This marks a significant rise from the 2.1% recorded a year prior.

Energy prices were the largest contributor to the euro area's annual inflation rate, adding 1.89 percentage points. Services contributed 1.55 percentage points, while non-energy industrial goods and food, alcohol & tobacco also showed positive contributions.

Among Member States, Romania recorded the highest annual rate at 7.0%, followed by Lithuania at 6.1% and Bulgaria at 5.9%. Conversely, Sweden reported the lowest rate at 0.6%, with Czechia and Denmark both at 2.1%.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

body: The $60m (£45m) plane was destroyed in an hours-long raid by an anti-war protester, according to the FBI.

articles.headline: US loses measles elimination status after 26 years amid record case numbers
body: States have reported over 5,400 cases and 10 measles-related deaths for the first time since the early 1990s.

articles.headline: American soldier arrested by UK police on suspicion of spying taken into US military custody
body: The Metropolitan Police say he has been taken into custody by the US Military over suspected national security and espionage allegations.

articles.headline: Palestinian woman, 72, shot dead by Israeli settlers in West Bank, health ministry says
body: Palestinians say there was an attack by settlers in al-Duyuk al-Tahta, while the Israeli military says the settlers fired after being attacked.

articles.headline: William and Kate celebrate Earthshot Prize winners in Mumbai
body: The Prince and Princess of Wales were joined by sporting and acting stars for the annual environmental awards ceremony.

articles.headline: New video shows explosions moments before part of Crimea Bridge collapses
body: BBC Verify analyses footage showing the final moments before part of the bridge fell and videos showing the scale of destruction.
